title: Maximum Profitable Triplets With Increasing Prices II
statement:
There are `n` items in a row. Item `i` has price `prices[i]` and would bring in profit `profits[i]`.

Choose three positions `i < j < k` such that the prices go strictly up along them: `prices[i] < prices[j] < prices[k]`. The value of the choice is `profits[i] + profits[j] + profits[k]`.

Return the largest value over all such choices. If no three positions have strictly rising prices, return `-1`.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying all triples is O(n³), far too slow for 50,000 items. Fix the middle item `j` instead: the best triple through it pairs `profits[j]` with the largest profit among earlier items priced below `prices[j]` and the largest profit among later items priced above it. Those two numbers are "maximum over a range of prices" questions, and prices are at most 5000, so a Fenwick tree indexed by price that stores maximums answers each one in O(log P).

## Approach

1. Let `maxPrice` be the largest price. `update` raises a tree slot and its covering slots to a value; `query` returns the maximum stored over prices `1..index`.
2. Sweep left to right. Before inserting item `j`, `leftBest[j]` is the query up to `prices[j] - 1`, the best cheaper item before it. Then insert `profits[j]` at `prices[j]`.
3. Sweep right to left with a fresh tree. Store each price at `flipped = maxPrice + 1 - price`, so higher prices land on smaller indices and "more expensive" becomes a prefix query up to `flipped - 1`.
4. When both `leftBest[j]` and `rightBest` are positive (profits are at least 1, so 0 means "none"), update `answer` with the triple's total.
5. Return `answer`, which stays `-1` if no middle item had both neighbours.

## Example 1, step by step

`prices = [10, 2, 3, 4]`, `profits = [100, 2, 7, 10]`. The left sweep gives `leftBest = [0, 0, 2, 7]`: price 3 sees price 2 (profit 2), and price 4 sees prices 2 and 3 (best 7). The right sweep starts at price 4 with nothing to its right. At price 3, the item priced 4 is later and dearer, so `rightBest = 10` and `answer = 2 + 7 + 10 = 19`. Price 2 has `leftBest = 0` and price 10 has nothing dearer, so the answer is `19`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log P), with P the largest price: two sweeps, each doing one query and one update per item.
- Space: O(n + P) for `leftBest` and the two trees.

## Pitfalls

- Prices must rise strictly, so query up to `prices[j] - 1` (and `flipped - 1`), not the price itself.
- Query before updating, otherwise item `j` could pair with itself.
- A max-Fenwick tree only answers prefixes; the suffix side needs the flipped index or a second tree built from the right.
- Only middles with a valid item on both sides count; returning 0 instead of `-1` is wrong.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `maxPrice` | largest price, the size of each tree |
| `leftTree`, `rightTree` | Fenwick trees of maximum profit by (flipped) price |
| `leftBest[j]` | best profit of an earlier, cheaper item than `j` |
| `flipped` | `prices[j]` mirrored so dearer prices get smaller indices |
| `rightBest` | best profit of a later, dearer item than `j` |
| `answer` | best triple total so far, or `-1` |
